tagline: Colonial roads, plantation histories and a separate trail beside the James
intro: Route 5 generally follows the James River’s north bank between Richmond and Williamsburg, along the paths of older colonial roads. Outside those two cities, its entire length is a Virginia Byway. The Virginia Capital Trail largely parallels it in a separate paved lane for walking and cycling, crossing streams and marshy ground on wooden bridges. The highway passes a sequence of historic James River plantations, including Berkeley, Westover and Sherwood Forest.

The state assembled this road in pieces, beginning in 1923 with a stretch west from Charles City toward Richmond numbered Route 41. The Richmond–Williamsburg connection was complete in 1932 and became part of Route 5 in the 1933 renumbering. The Commonwealth Transportation Board designated Route 5 a Virginia Byway in 1975. The completed Capital Trail opened in October 2015, adding a dedicated route for cyclists and pedestrians.

Traveling east from Richmond, the corridor leads through Henrico into Charles City County, passing Shirley and then Berkeley and Westover. At Charles City, Route 155 meets the byway beside the county’s courthouse-centered community. Sherwood Forest lies farther east along the plantation sequence. Before Williamsburg, the Judith Stewart Dresser Bridge crosses the Chickahominy into James City County, a fixed span that succeeded the ferry and former drawbridge.

moments.title: Berkeley Plantation
moments.text: At Berkeley’s old wharf, Harrison’s Landing, Oliver W. Norton and General Daniel Butterfield wrote the melody of Taps in 1862; Norton first played the bugle call there. Union troops occupied the plantation that year. The site’s earlier history includes the 110 people Benjamin Harrison V held in slavery when he died in 1791. John Jamieson bought Berkeley in 1907 after having served there as a drummer boy in McClellan’s army; his son later restored the house. The mansion’s ground floor became a museum in the 1960s. The original quarters for enslaved people no longer survived when filmmakers built reconstructions for Harriet in 2018.

moments.title: Charles City
moments.text: Charles City’s courthouse remains at the center of the community where Routes 5 and 155 meet. Earlier county courthouses stood along the James at Westover and City Point before the court moved to this inland community. The old courthouse survives, but judicial use ended in 2007 and a new courthouse has been built. Charles City remains the county seat and a center for services including the library and post office. Here the Capital Trail briefly shares Courthouse Road near the government complex. The community lies about two miles north of the James River, between Richmond and Williamsburg.

moments.title: Sherwood Forest Plantation
moments.text: John Tyler gave Sherwood Forest its name in 1842, saying it signified that the Whig party had outlawed him. Tyler bought the plantation from his cousin Collier Minge; the house has remained in the Tyler family since that 1842 purchase. He retired here after leaving the White House in 1845. The plantation grew and processed tobacco using the labor of dozens of enslaved African Americans. Recorded surnames of enslaved people include Armistead, Hall, Black and Short. The house stretches 301 feet, including a long, narrow ballroom Tyler added for the Virginia reel. Restorers in the 1970s retained homemade storm windows after records identified them as Tyler’s work.
